paras: The death of William Rice occurred at Lawrenceville, Virginia, in late February 1903, when the body of the Black hotel worker was found beneath a railroad trestle over Rose creek. The local Brunswick Gazette, reprinted by the Richmond Planet, reported that several white men had beaten and whipped him, while a Washington paper reported that the coroner's jury found he died from a fall. An investigation at the county court in May found nothing.
Rice worked at the Southern Hotel in Lawrenceville, as a porter according to the Gazette and as head waiter according to the Washington Times. The Gazette called him "a highly respected colored man."

On the night before the body was found, members of the True Reformers, a Black charitable society, were walking home along Main Street from their monthly meeting. Near the court house square, they saw "several white men engaged in an alteration [altercation] of some kind with the man Rice." Rice's body was found on the morning of February 26 under the bridge at a spot where a cross tie was missing, some forty or fifty feet below the track.

Searchers then followed a trail from the street to the railroad, finding a pool of blood and torn hair, drops of blood on the steps, and a bloody collar. Farther on, according to the Gazette, Rice's shirt had been removed and switches cut from the shrubbery used on his bare back, and a second spot showed that he had been "again inhumanly beaten." The body had wounds on both sides of the head "apparently inflicted by a bludgeon" and a shattered jaw, which the Gazette attributed to the fall.

The Gazette wrote that the coroner's jury had first leaned toward an accidental fall but had returned no verdict and still had the matter under consideration. At the county court term that ended in early May, a number of witnesses were examined, but "nothing could be found out." No report of arrests or a trial was found.

The white papers gave the death a few lines. Under the headline "Tragedy at Lawrenceville," the Washington Times of February 28 called Rice "a negro head waiter," mentioned a revolver with three chambers empty near the body, and gave the coroner's finding of a fall without mention of a beating. In May the Richmond Times-Dispatch noted the fruitless inquiry in one sentence of a Lawrenceville court column.

The Richmond Planet put the Gazette's full account on its front page on March 14 under the headline "William Rice a Most Respectable Colored Man," adding that developments pointed "Conclusively to the Fact of Foul Play." The reprinted text argued that there was no moral difference between killing Rice and forcing him to walk the trestle, and called it "the dark and bloody deed" that had brought disgrace on the town.

The cause of death was disputed: the Washington Times reported a coroner's finding of a fall, while the Gazette, the local and fuller account, said the jury had expressed that view before the blood trail was found and had not returned a verdict. The two also differ on timing, with the Washington Times saying he was found late Wednesday night and the Gazette saying the morning of February 26.

reader.title: Death of William Rice
bases: The Brunswick Gazette reported that several white men beat and whipped Rice before his body was found under a trestle (A2, A3), while the coroner's jury was reported to attribute the death to a fall (A1), so the beating is reported but whether it killed him is disputed.

Rice's death beneath the railroad bridge is reported by three independent texts (A1, A2, A4), but the Gazette's account of a beating by white men (A2, A3) is contradicted by the coroner's jury's reported finding of death from a fall (A1), and a later investigation found nothing (A4).

accounts.label: Brunswick Gazette (Lawrenceville), reprinted by the Richmond Planet
accounts.gist: Rice was beaten and whipped by several white men along a trail from Main Street to the railroad, then either killed and dropped through the trestle or forced to walk it; the death was 'foul play', not accident.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury (as reported by the Washington Times)
accounts.gist: Rice came to his death from a fall; a revolver with three chambers empty was found ten feet from the body.

accounts.label: Times-Dispatch Lawrenceville correspondent
accounts.gist: A court investigation examined witnesses in May but nothing could be found out.

framing.detail: The Richmond Planet ran the Gazette text on its front page under 'William Rice a Most Respectable Colored Man' and 'Subsequent Developments Point Conclusively to the Fact of Foul Play,' with the Gazette calling it 'the dark and bloody deed.'
The Washington Times gave three sentences headed 'Tragedy at Lawrenceville,' calling Rice 'a negro head waiter' and reporting the coroner's finding of a fall with no mention of a beating.
The Times-Dispatch noted the case in one sentence of a Lawrenceville court column, subheaded 'Investigation of Case of William Rice at Lawrenceville Results in Nothing.'

versions.value: beating by several white men, followed by a fall or being dropped through the trestle; jury had returned no verdict

conflicts.note: The Gazette says the jury at first expressed the belief that he fell but returned no verdict after the trail of blood was found; the Washington Times may report that first expression. The Gazette is the local and fuller account.
The Gazette places the beating the night before the body was found.
